title: The Next Good Thing Is Not a Promise
subtitle: A three-minute anticipation practice makes room for one small, already-planned moment ahead—without requiring optimism, excitement or a better mood.
imageAlt: Two friends sit together at a kitchen table, each holding a mug as one describes a book they plan to read.
imageConcept: Two friends at a familiar kitchen table in late afternoon light, mugs between them; one gestures toward a paperback while the other listens, suggesting an ordinary plan worth anticipating without making it grand.
body: There is a particular pleasure in knowing that something ordinary is waiting for you: a song on the drive home, the first chapter of a book, a familiar lunch, or a conversation already on the calendar. Thinking ahead can be enjoyable in its own right, even before the event arrives. But anticipation is easy to turn into another assignment: find something exciting, picture it perfectly, and use the thought to feel better. That is not the point of this practice. Choose one modest event that is already feasible, give it a little attention, and let the experience be whatever it is. It may bring interest, pleasure, worry, mixed feelings or no noticeable response. A future moment is not a promise about how you will feel; it is simply something you can notice approaching.

Psychologist Fred B. Bryant describes savoring as attending to positive experience across three time frames: anticipating something positive, noticing it as it unfolds, and remembering it afterward. Those are related but distinct ways of engaging with experience; this exercise focuses only on the first. Bryant also notes that deliberately seeking or creating positive experiences—a more proactive form of savoring—needs further study. That matters because a useful idea is not automatically a proven intervention, and a three-minute exercise should not be presented as treatment or a reliable way to reduce stress. Think of it instead as a small attention ritual: a chance to notice what is ahead without demanding that it deliver a particular emotional result. [1]

A modest plan gives the imagination something concrete to work with, without requiring a purchase, a special occasion or a change to the calendar. It can be a meal you already intend to make, the next time you will call someone, a walk along a familiar route, or ten minutes with a hobby after work. Specificity helps: “the song I’ll play on the way back” offers a detail to picture; “I’ll have a great evening” is a forecast that may be hard to control. In experiments, participants who anticipated a positive event reported more positive emotion around a social stress task. The research used controlled laboratory activities and student participants, so it supports the possibility that anticipation can matter—not a claim that this everyday exercise will reliably improve anyone’s mood or coping. [2]

First, pick a small event in the next few days that is already planned or genuinely easy to do. Avoid choosing something that depends on another person changing their mind, a purchase you cannot make, or an outcome you cannot control. For about a minute, picture one detail: where you might be, what you might hear, the feel of a warm mug, or the first line of a book. Keep the picture loose; there is no need to script the whole event. Then spend a moment naming what is present now. You might feel eager, mildly curious, uncertain, distracted or nothing in particular. Finally, let the thought go and return to what you were doing. If the image brings up worry or disappointment, stop or choose a different, more neutral plan. The exercise is optional, not a test.
If you do it with someone

Two people can take turns without becoming each other’s motivational coach. One person shares a small thing they are looking forward to; the other can ask, “What part are you looking forward to?” Then switch. A listener might hear that their friend is anticipating the quiet of an early walk, not a full weekend itinerary. The helpful response is to stay with what was actually said: “The first few minutes sound good,” or simply, “I’m glad you have that.” Avoid upgrading the plan, offering to organize it, or promising it will be wonderful. Those moves can turn a modest moment into an obligation. Either person can pass, keep the answer brief, or say the feeling is complicated. Sharing is an option, not a requirement, and the listener does not need to solve anything.

Positive anticipation can sit beside real uncertainty. A planned visit might be welcome and tiring; a workday might include one enjoyable break and several difficult hours. If you notice yourself trying to guarantee the best version of the event, return to a detail you can actually expect, such as the route, the familiar room or the time set aside. Then leave the rest open. Research on anticipation and recall has examined how people’s appraisals of pleasant activities relate to their reported feelings; experiments on “dampening” appraisals offer a reason not to turn the exercise into pressure to think positively. They do not establish that this practice will help every person. If looking ahead makes you feel worse, you can stop, choose something neutral, or skip the exercise altogether. [3]

Try this once with a moment already on your calendar: the first song on a commute, the next chapter, a meal you have planned, or a conversation you expect to have. Sit or stand somewhere you can pause comfortably. Give the event one concrete detail and a minute of attention; name whatever feeling is there, including none. If someone is with you, let them share without fixing or improving the plan. Then close the exercise and carry on. When the moment arrives, it may be different from the picture, and that is not failure. The point is not to manufacture happiness in advance or grade the event afterward. It is to give a small, real thing on the horizon a little room in your attention—and leave its meaning open.
